role: On-site data collector at a robot data collection factory
headline: Two years at a milk tea shop, then in through a day-rate gig to a robot data collection factory in Minhang, Shanghai: wearing a head camera and motion-capture gloves, folding clothes, wiping tables and picking up cups again and again in life-size kitchens, supermarkets and bedrooms, and now learning VR teleoperation
unit: A robot data collection factory in Minhang, Shanghai: several thousand square meters of factory floor fitted with dozens of life-size home, retail and workstation scenes, collecting training data for several robotics companies
level: You can get the wearable rig on in two minutes and could do the folding, table-wiping and pick-and-place task packs with your eyes closed, with a pass rate in your team's top five. You've only had twenty hours of VR teleoperation on the real robot, and still get dizzy if you wear the headset too long
intro: A year ago a recruiting app showed you a day-rate gig: fold clothes wearing a camera, ¥30 an hour. You thought it was a scam; you went, and it was real, and half the people who went with you quit on the first day. You stayed. Now you're in a fake kitchen putting the same cup into the same dishwasher three hundred times a day, and every time has to be like the first. As of today, you're going to learn to direct a real robot with a pair of controllers.
salary_note: Estimate: an on-site collector at a Shanghai data collection factory, paid by valid hours and pass rate plus a night-shift allowance, earns about thirty percent above the national figure. In months between projects there are fewer hours, and pay drops back to the national figure.

facts.label: On-Site Data Collector / Teleoperator (current level)
facts.value: 6 months-2 years, ¥4,641–6,825 a month (national average, estimated from pay by experience)

facts.label: Next level up
facts.value: Collection Team Leader / Data QC (1-3 years)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Putting on the rig and doing a trial collection on your first day

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Teleoperating a real robot through grasping tasks on the night shift

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 3 related job listings nationwide, 1 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: Clock in, collect your gear. Head camera, two wrist cameras, a pair of motion-capture gloves: you put them on one by one and run a calibration on the tablet, and on screen your hands become a skeleton.
Today's task pack: load dishes into the dishwasher in kitchen scene one, three hundred times. You roll your sleeves up to the elbow, check that both hands are in frame, and tap start.

The team lead comes to change the scene variables: the tablecloth goes from white to checked, the lights down a notch, the cup swapped for a blue one. You keep going. Your movements can't be too fast, or too perfect; they have to be like at home.
A ¥15 boxed lunch in the canteen. Beside you are a man who used to deliver food and a retired woman, who says she came because she can't sit still at home, and she's folded clothes her whole life.
QC has bounced twelve of your clips from the morning: left hand out of frame, motion interrupted. You watch the playback; it's where you stopped to scratch your face.

Teleoperation training. You put on the VR headset and pick up the controllers, and the two-armed robot across the room moves with your hands. You want it to pick up an apple; its gripper hangs over the apple for half a second before it closes.
Too long in VR, and you feel a bit sick. You take it off and stand in the corridor for five minutes. Outside the window are rows of identical factory buildings, some lit with the same white lights.

Home on the metro to your rented room, wrists aching a little. On your phone you see a news story about a company whose robot has learned to fold clothes, and the shirt in the video is a color you think you've folded.

ladder.title: Part-Time / At-Home Data Collector
ladder.focus: Wear the rig and collect by task pack, paid by the day or by the hour.

ladder.title: On-Site Data Collector / Teleoperator
ladder.focus: Teleoperation at the collection center, setting up scenes, uploading.

ladder.title: Collection Team Leader / Data QC
ladder.focus: Quality checking, first-pass screening, leading a small team.

ladder.title: Collection Planner / Data Operations
ladder.focus: Project planning and working with the algorithm teams.

ladder.title: Data Collection Project Lead
ladder.focus: Running multiple projects across multiple sites.

ai_tasks.name: Putting on the rig and doing a trial collection on your first day
ai_tasks.how: AI can't help you wear the gear or do the trial collection; that's down to a person's hands and how well they adapt. At most AI can check afterward whether frames were dropped and the streams are in sync. A person gets the rig on firmly, does the movements right, and decides whether to stay.

ai_tasks.name: Recording a full eight hours of folding clothes at home
ai_tasks.how: A real person has to fold clothes at home on camera for eight straight hours, with their own body and their own patience. AI can only flag in the background whether the view is blocked or a device has dropped out; the person keeps the movements natural and steady.

ai_tasks.name: Teleoperating a real robot through grasping tasks on the night shift
ai_tasks.how: AI can help with trajectory planning, automatic obstacle avoidance and recognizing what's in view, lightening the load. A person on the night shift controls the robot remotely, deals with things like slipping grips and jams, and is responsible for the quality of the data.

ai_tasks.name: Collecting in a real supermarket
ai_tasks.how: A supermarket is a real, open scene with shoppers and staff, so you have to talk to people, move around the crowd and do your picking and placing in front of the shelves. AI can only check the data afterward; the coordinating and the movements on site are all down to a person.

ai_tasks.name: Setting up a scene from the variables list
ai_tasks.how: AI can suggest scene combinations from the variables list and count the gaps in lighting and background coverage in the existing data. A person actually changes the lights and backdrops and places the objects, and judges which changes really matter.

ai_tasks.name: Quality-checking a batch of video and bouncing clips
ai_tasks.how: AI can automatically screen for common problems like blur, dropped frames, desync, occlusion and interrupted motion, and give a first-pass result. A person only needs to spot-check AI's calls, handle the disputed clips, and review the final rejections.

ai_tasks.name: Leading a team of new hires through a project
ai_tasks.how: AI can compile each person's daily progress, pass rate and common mistakes and generate a training outline. A person demonstrates on site, leads people, answers questions, and delivers the task pack on time and answers for it.

events.e_first_week: Of the twenty people who started with you, a month later only six are left. Some say it's too boring, some say their hands hurt. You don't find it boring; you count how many more clips pass each day than the day before.
events.e_vr_sick: Three days straight of teleoperation, and in VR you get so dizzy you throw up once. The team lead has you take it off for ten minutes every forty, and you do; by the second week you get dizzy less.
events.e_wrist: A month of folding clothes, and your right wrist starts to hurt; you can't wring out a towel. The doctor says it's tendinitis and to avoid repetitive movements. You laugh and say repetitive movements are my job.
events.e_robot_learns: Someone from the algorithm team comes to the floor and plays a video: the robot folding a T-shirt on its own for the first time, crookedly. He says twenty thousand of your clips are in that. Everyone applauds, and you applaud longest.
events.e_night: A project is behind schedule, and you're put on a month of night-shift teleoperation. At three in the morning the vast factory floor holds only a few robots and a few people; you guide one to pick up a bottle of soy sauce, and it's so quiet you can hear the motors.
events.e_supermarket: You're sent to a real supermarket for an outdoor collection, picking and placing goods from the shelves among the shoppers. An old man asks if you're filming a short video. You say you're teaching a robot to shop, and he asks whether it'll learn to haggle.
events.e_new_job_title: The news says the state has officially listed your job as a new occupation. You screenshot it into the family group chat, and your mother asks: so does that mean it counts as a proper job now? You say it does.
events.e_love: A teleoperator on the next team glances over from a distance every time your robot gets stuck. Later the two of you go cycling along the riverside, and he says he thinks you're the gentlest at handling robots.
events.e_ai_qc: QC switches to an AI first pass: blur, dropped frames, occlusion, interrupted motion, it flags them in seconds. More of your clips get bounced, but every reason is spelled out, and one look at the playback tells you what went wrong.
events.e_dry_spell: A big client's project ends and the next isn't signed, and for a month the factory schedules only half the hours. You do the math on rent and work two weeks of odd shifts at the milk tea shop downstairs.
events.e_glove: A batch of force-feedback gloves arrives, and with them on you can feel how hard the robot's gripper is pressing on things. The first time you pick up an egg through the robot and it doesn't break, you laugh out loud inside the VR.
events.e_failure_data: The algorithm team says what the robots lack most isn't data on doing it right, but data on how to recover from doing it wrong. You start letting the cup slip on purpose, letting the shirt fall, and rescuing them, over and over.
events.e_eyes: Years in VR and watching playback, and your short sight gets worse by another hundred degrees. You get new glasses, and have to press the frames tighter under the VR headset.
events.e_house_rent: Your landlord sells the flat and you move again, to an old estate further out in Xinzhuang. On moving day you fold all your own clothes, so fast and so neat the friends helping you just stare.
events.e_sim: Simulation and video generation become the trend for making data, and some say real-robot collection won't need as many people from now on. The factory goes from three hundred collectors to two hundred, and the ones who stay do the work simulation can't do well.
events.e_wedding: You go home to Fuyang for the wedding. A younger cousin asks what you do in Shanghai; you say you teach robots to do housework. He says so you won't have to do any at home, and you say it's the opposite.
events.e_mentor: A new hire you're training has a pass rate of only forty percent her first week. You watch playback with her for three days, teaching her not to let her hands hog the camera, not to move too perfectly. The second week she's at eighty percent, and buys you a milk tea.
events.e_baby: Your daughter is born. The first thing she learns is to grab, and you watch her reach, open, close, and think of all the grippers you've taught.
events.e_robot_home: In a mall you see a home robot demonstrating clearing a table, and you recognize the way it puts a cup into the dishwasher: that's your technique. You stand at the back of the crowd and watch a long time.
events.e_neck: Years of wearing a head camera, and your neck goes first; after a while looking down it goes numb. You stick a note on your station: look up once an hour.
events.e_parent: Your mother goes into hospital in Fuyang, and you take a week off. The care worker in the ward is turning an old patient, and watching her hands you find yourself thinking: how many clips would it take to teach a robot that move.
events.e_spec: The scene variables list and task pack standards you led the writing of are rolled out by the company to three new collection centers in other cities. When a new center opens, the first thing in every team leader's hands is that.

c_teleop.title: Specialize in teleoperation, or stay with wearable collection
c_teleop.situation: The team lead says teleoperation is short of people: VR headset and controllers, directing the real robot, ¥10 more an hour than wearable collection, and lots of night shifts. But you get dizzy if you wear it too long, and you'd have to practice dozens more hours to make the grade.

options.label: Go train in teleoperation
options.result: You practice two hours a day, taking it off when you're dizzy and putting it back on when you've recovered. A month later you guide the robot to pull a pen out of a jumble of objects, first try.

options.label: Stay with wearable collection
options.result: You say your hands are steadier than any controller. Your pass rate stays in the team's top three, but the teleoperators get more hours scheduled than you.

c_home_collect.title: Go home and do crowdsourced collection
c_home_collect.situation: The company has started an at-home collection program: they ship a rig to your home, and you fold clothes and tidy tables in your own place by task pack, on your own schedule, paid by valid hours. No more crowded metro, but no team lead, no coworkers and no social insurance either.

options.label: Go home and crowdsource
options.result: You carry the rig back to your rented room and wipe your own little table over and over. Your time is your own now, and so are the long days alone in front of the camera.
options.end: You became an at-home collector, taking task packs from a few more platforms, folding clothes, wiping tables and tidying bookshelves in your rented room. Later you moved, and set up that camera in your new living room too.

options.label: Stay at the factory
options.result: You say you like the people at the factory. In the canteen the retired woman tells you she doesn't want to go home either; at home it's just her, folding clothes alone.

options.label: Take a bit extra at home on weekends
options.result: Weekdays at the factory, weekends taking at-home task packs, over ¥1,000 more a month. Your wardrobe becomes the tidiest in the building.

c_qc.title: Compete for Collection Team Leader / Data QC
c_qc.situation: The factory is promoting a few collectors to team leaders and QC. A team leader takes a dozen people through a project; QC reviews other people's data and argues it out with the AI's first-pass results. To compete you hand in a list of data problems you've found, and judge a set of disputed clips on the spot.

options.label: Put your name in
options.result: Your list sets out seventeen common reasons clips get bounced, each with a playback example. On the disputed set, your calls differ from the panel's by just one clip.

options.label: Collect another year
options.result: You don't think you can yet manage women twenty years older than you, and don't apply. The new team leader is the man who used to deliver food, and when he does the roster he always saves you the easy task packs.

c_trainer.title: Move into embodied AI robot training
c_trainer.situation: A partner robotics company wants to poach a few skilled people from the data factory as robot trainers: demonstrating in their lab, tuning movements, watching the model's success rate. Thirty percent more pay, a bit of programming to learn, and an hour and a half from where you live now.

options.label: Go to the robotics company
options.result: For the first time you sit beside an algorithm engineer watching the success rate curve on screen. They ask why the robot always slips at the same point in its grasp, and you say its hand is too fast.

options.label: Stay at the data factory
options.result: You say you know the people and the scenes here. The robotics people say they'll still come to you with questions, and you add them to your work group chat.

c_ai_qc.title: Learn to calibrate the AI QC
c_ai_qc.situation: AI quality checking keeps getting more accurate, and the company wants someone to calibrate it full time: spot-checking its calls, handling disputed clips, feeding it new rejection rules. Your supervisor wants you, but some say once it's calibrated, they won't need as many QC staff.

options.label: Go calibrate the AI
options.result: You find the AI has been treating a perfectly natural pause as an interrupted motion and bouncing a whole batch of good data. You write three rules for the algorithm team, and the next week its misjudgments drop by half.

options.label: Keep leading collection
options.result: You say you'd rather be in the scenes. Someone else sets the AI's rules; there's one you think is wrong, and you raise it at the weekly meeting.

c_planner.title: Become Collection Planner / Data Operations
c_planner.situation: The company wants a collection planner to take requirements from the algorithm teams, break them into task packs, schedule sites and people, and track each project's progress and pass rate. Take it, and you stop going into the scenes to collect; every day it's schedules and data dashboards.

options.label: Take the planner job
options.result: You start attending the algorithm team's weekly data review, listening to where the model falls short and coming back to break it into task packs. The last time you put on gloves yourself was two months ago.

options.label: You'd rather lead a team
options.result: You turn it down, saying you still like being in the scenes. The new planner is a graduate student, and before breaking down a task pack he often comes to ask how many times a person can do a given movement in a day.

c_ops_tech.title: Go into robot field maintenance
c_ops_tech.situation: A company selling robots into factories and supermarkets is hiring field maintenance technicians: people who understand how robots move, where they tend to jam and how to do first fixes. You'd travel to customer sites across the country for twenty percent more pay.

options.label: Go into maintenance
options.result: With a case of tools and a laptop you board a high-speed train to a factory in Suzhou.
options.end: You became a robot field maintenance technician, watching the movements you once collected data for being done over and over in real factories and supermarkets. When a robot's hand trembles, you can tell at a glance.

options.label: Stay in data collection
options.result: You say your child is still small and you don't want to be on the road. The company says they'll ask you in to train people sometime, and you say fine.

c_new_site.title: Go to the new collection center in Hefei
c_new_site.situation: The company has opened a new collection center in Hefei and wants you to lead the team and build the scenes from scratch, for ten percent more pay and halfway closer to your home in Fuyang. Your child is in kindergarten in Shanghai, and your husband works in Shanghai.

options.label: Go to Hefei
options.result: In an empty factory building in Hefei, starting with buying tablecloths and cups, you build thirty scenes one by one. On weekends you take the train back to Shanghai, or go to Fuyang to see your parents.

options.label: Stay in Shanghai
options.result: You say keeping the family together matters most. The company sends someone else, who calls to ask how to sequence the scene variables, and you talk her through it for an hour.

c_project_head.title: Become Data Collection Project Lead
c_project_head.situation: The company wants one person to run several cities' collection centers and several clients' projects, negotiating requirements, prices and data standards with robotics companies. That means half your time in meetings and half on the road, and if there's a major data quality problem, you're the first one asked.

options.label: Take it on
options.result: You start visiting clients, writing quotes and answering the algorithm teams' questions at reviews. Every time you reach a new center, you still put on the gloves first and collect one clip yourself.

options.label: Hand it to someone younger
options.result: You recommend a team leader you trained. The first call she makes after taking over is to ask how the lighting should vary in a new scene.

endings.retire: On your last day you put on a pair of gloves again. There are far fewer people in the collection center than back then, but twice as many scenes, and half the work is done by robots on their own while people watch. In kitchen scene one you put a cup into the dishwasher, very slowly, the way you did the first time. You take off the gloves and upload one last clip to the platform.
endings.burnout: That winter your wrist and neck give out together; you can't wear a head camera or hold a controller. The company moves you to training and records, compiling the task pack standards of all these years. When you teach new hires, your first line is still: don't let your hands hog the camera, don't move too perfectly.

stages: You're on site at the collection center, half the day doing wearable collection and half teleoperating the real robot. You set up scenes by task pack, change the variables, calibrate head and wrist cameras, and upload and tag clip after clip on the collection platform; when QC bounces a clip, you watch the playback yourself and find out why. The team lead schedules your hours by pass rate, and now and then someone from the algorithm team comes to look at your hands.

You lead a collection team of a dozen-odd and double as QC. Every morning you hand out task packs and assign scenes by project, by day you move between scenes correcting movements, in the afternoon you review a batch of data against the AI's first-pass results, and on disputes your word is final; a new hire's first-week playback you watch with them, clip by clip. You now hold a roster and a daily pass-rate report.

You liaise with several robotics companies' algorithm teams. Every week you sit in on data reviews, hearing which movements the model fails at, then come back and break it into task packs and scene variable lists, scheduling sites, people and timelines; you watch every project's pass rate and delivery date, and explain to clients why this batch is two days late. You rarely put on gloves anymore.

You run collection centers in several cities and a dozen-odd projects. You negotiate requirements and prices with clients, set data standards and compliance rules, decide which center builds which scenes and how many people to hire; at an industry conference someone asks if real-robot data is still needed, and you tell them about a robot rescuing a slipping cup.
work: The team lead has you redo bedroom three from the variables list: navy sheets, a warm-light lamp, one more pillow. When you're done you photograph and upload it, and another line on the list is ticked off.

During teleoperation the robot's left arm suddenly locks up. By the rules you let go of the controllers and call maintenance. The technician checks it and says a joint overheated, and you note the downtime in the collection log.

A woman trying out for the job can't get her head camera on straight; the lens keeps tilting. You adjust her strap and tell her not to tuck her chin so hard when she looks down, and her second clip passes.

The QC system fails a folding clip for interrupted motion. You watch the playback: the collector stopped to smooth down the collar. You pass it, and write in the notes: this is something a real person does.

A project needs five thousand supermarket pick-and-place clips in three days. You split the team into three shifts and keep the hardest scene, the chilled cabinets, yourself, and on the last night everything's in by ten.
A new hire just out of the army moves too perfectly, exactly the same every time. You tell him the algorithm wants human, not machine, and to imagine he's picking things up at home.

The algorithm team says the model keeps failing to pick up transparent cups. You come back and break it into a task pack: twenty kinds of clear containers, five lighting setups, three table surfaces, nine thousand clips in all.

A client comes to the factory for acceptance and samples a hundred clips; three have misaligned timestamps. You pull the raw logs on the spot, find a wrist camera's clock drifted, and retag that whole batch.
Writing the variables list for a new scene, you stop at item forty and go stand in the convenience store downstairs for an hour, watching how real people take things off the shelves.

A robotics company comes to negotiate its annual contract and wants to cut the unit price by thirty percent. You lay out each center's pass and rework rates, and in the end it comes down ten percent, with a new clause on compensation for data quality.
Legal points out that outdoor collection videos have captured passers-by's faces. You set a new rule: all outdoor data gets anonymized before it's uploaded.
The AI planning system proposes a scene configuration for a new center. You walk the site with two planners, cut five scenes, and add a ward in a care home.
past: You finish middle school in Fuyang, Anhui, missing the top high school by a few points. Your mother says an ordinary high school is fine; get into a vocational college, then go to a big city.

In the gaokao (college entrance exam) you get into e-commerce at a vocational college in Hefei. You learn to shoot product photos and write listings, and what you like best is shooting clothes laid flat, folded perfectly neat.
After graduation you follow a classmate to Shanghai and do customer service for an online shop, which folds three months later. You go to work at a milk tea shop, ten hours a day on your feet.
The shop manager says your hands are fast, one of you is worth two. You learn to seal cups with your eyes closed, but your pay won't go up, though the rent does.

On a recruiting app you find a day-rate gig: fold clothes wearing a camera, ¥30 an hour. On your trial day half the people who came with you leave. You fold clothes all afternoon and think it isn't hard.

late.pension_note: Estimate: Shanghai's basic pension for company employees, nothing paid in your first year or two of day-rate work and then contributions on the company's wage base once you were on site, comes to a little over forty percent of your final monthly pay.
scenes: For the first few months of retirement, doing housework, you still keep both hands in front of you out of habit, as if a camera were watching. You smile and let your hands relax.
Your family buys a home robot. When it clears the table and puts the cups into the dishwasher you watch from beside it, and say its wrist is still too stiff.

Your daughter gets into university to study robotics engineering. She says a lecture covered data collection, and the video the teacher played had a pair of hands folding clothes that looked like yours.
On a trip back to Fuyang, your mother has grown old and folds clothes slowly. You sit beside her and help, piece by piece, no camera, just as neat.
No more head camera, and slowly your neck gets better. The first morning you take your daughter to school, you stand at the gate a long time.
A young team leader at the collection center calls: a new task pack keeps getting a low pass rate. You hear her out and tell her to check first whether the lighting is too bright.
When the time comes you retire. The task pack standards you wrote are still in use, and nobody has changed the line on the first page.
In your first year away from the collection center, whenever you fold clothes, you find yourself counting which one this is.
You find your footing in the new place. Passing those factory buildings in Minhang now and then, the white lights inside are still on, and you don't know who's folding clothes in there now.
The new hire you trained becomes a project lead and speaks at an industry conference. She says when she started, a team leader told her: the algorithm wants human, not machine.

Later robots get better and better at work, folding clothes, wiping tables, picking up cups, no longer news. Only you know that every one of their movements was first done thousands of times by a person.
Your grandson asks what you used to do. You say you taught robots to do housework. He asks if you managed to teach them, and you think a moment and say, a little.

closing.retire: One evening many years later you're washing dishes in the kitchen while the home robot wipes the table beside you. It knocks a cup so it wobbles, then reaches out and steadies it. You stop with a bowl in your hands and watch it, and after a while go back to washing.
closing.burnout: Many years later you find an old pair of motion-capture gloves in a cupboard, the paint worn off the fingertip sensors. You put them on to try, make a fist, then take them off and put them back.
closing.end: Many years later, in a mall, you see a robot folding clothes, fast and neat. The crowd around it is filming; you watch from the back a while, and think the way it folds the collar looks a little like you.
